tracks.title: Study Planner
tracks.brief: Build a personal Study Planner to manage fictional tasks and time budgets. Learn core Python concepts step by step.

steps.title: Greeting Function
steps.outcome: Learn to define a function, validate string input, and return a value.
steps.recap: Start here: a program follows written instructions. No earlier project step is needed.

blocks.title: A function receives a value and returns an answer
blocks.idea: def starts a reusable function. name is its input parameter. The indented return line sends an answer back; it does not display it. Calling print on that answer displays text.
trace: The + joins two strings, giving Hi Asha.
return sends that string back; print displays it.

blocks.title: Clean text, then reject an empty value
blocks.idea: strip removes only spaces at the outer ends. An if chooses a branch. raise ValueError stops invalid input; a caller can catch it. An all-space name becomes empty.
blocks.example:
name = ' Asha '
print(name.strip())  # Asha
trace: Start with spaces before and after Asha.
strip gives Asha without changing letters.
An empty cleaned name must raise ValueError, not return a greeting.

steps.mission: Write a greeting function that strips outer spaces and rejects empty names. Keep every earlier function and its input/output contract. Use fictional values only.
steps.code:
def greeting(name):
    # TODO: strip name, raise ValueError if empty, return 'Ready, '+name+'!'
    pass

# Demo
print(greeting(' Alice '))

blocks.title: A dictionary keeps related facts together
blocks.idea: Curly braces create a dictionary of key:value pairs. Keys such as title name a fact. task["title"] reads that fact. False is Python’s boolean for not completed; it is different from text "False".
blocks.example:
task = {'id': 1, 'title': 'Math', 'minutes': 30, 'done': False}
print(task['title'])  # Math
trace: One task has four named facts.
The title key maps to Math.
Reading that key returns Math, not the whole dictionary.

blocks.title: Check the boundaries before creating the task
blocks.idea: type(x) is int checks for an integer and rejects True/False as task numbers. 1 <= minutes <= 240 includes both ends. A valid task must have a positive id and a nonempty cleaned title.
blocks.example:
minutes = 240
print(type(minutes) is int and 1 <= minutes <= 240)  # True
trace: It meets the inclusive lower and upper bounds.
0,241 and text "30" must be rejected before creating the task.

blocks.title: Visit each task once

blocks.title: Keep the running total outside the loop
blocks.idea: An accumulator remembers an answer while the loop runs. total += value means total = total + value. An empty list leaves the starting total unchanged.

steps.title: Adding Tasks

blocks.title: Copy the list before appending
blocks.idea: list(tasks) creates a new list containing the same task objects. append adds to that new list. This is a shallow copy: it protects list membership, but does not clone the task dictionaries.
blocks.example:
tasks = [1]
new_tasks = list(tasks)
new_tasks.append(2)
print(tasks, new_tasks)  # [1] [1, 2]

blocks.title: Scan ids before adding
blocks.idea: A task id identifies one task, even if two titles match. Compare the incoming id with every existing id. A match must raise ValueError; do not silently add a duplicate.
blocks.example:
ids = [1, 2]
print(2 in ids)  # True
trace: Reject the addition; leave the original list unchanged.

blocks.title: Copy each dictionary before changing it
blocks.idea: A list copy alone still shares its dictionaries. dict(task) creates a new dictionary. Change done only on that copy so the original task remains untouched.
blocks.example:
task = {'done': False}
copy = dict(task)
copy['done'] = True
print(task['done'], copy['done'])  # False True

blocks.title: Remember whether the requested id was found
blocks.idea: Start found=False. In the loop, change it to True only when a task id matches. Check found after visiting all tasks; a missing id is a failure, not a silently unchanged result.
trace: Id1 does not match; id2 does.
After the loop, True confirms a match.

steps.title: Weekly Summary
steps.outcome: Learn list indexing and data aggregation.
steps.recap: Keep the earlier functions unchanged. This step adds one new capability to the same planner; the starter contains working earlier functions.

blocks.title: Seven days use indices zero through six
blocks.idea: [0]*7 creates seven totals. Day1 goes in slot0, so use day-1. A zero-minute session is valid; negative minutes and days outside1..7 are invalid.
blocks.example:
totals = [0] * 7
totals[1 - 1] += 20
print(totals)  # [20, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
trace: Add20 to that slot, leaving the other six at0.

blocks.title: Several sessions on one day add together
blocks.idea: Visit each session and add its minutes to its day’s slot. Validate day and minutes before indexing; day0 would otherwise use Python’s last-slot indexing.
blocks.example:
totals = [0] * 7
for minutes in [20, 10]:
    totals[0] += minutes
print(totals[0])  # 30
trace: The second adds10 to the same slot.
The day total is30, not only the most recent session.

steps.mission: Write weekly_summary(sessions) taking a list of {day: 1..7, minutes: >=0}. Return 7 totals. Keep every earlier function and its input/output contract. Use fictional values only.

steps.title: JSON Import/Export
steps.outcome: Learn serialization and robust data validation.
steps.recap: Keep the earlier functions unchanged. This step adds one new capability to the same planner; the starter contains working earlier functions.

blocks.title: JSON is text representing values
blocks.idea: import json brings in Python’s standard-library JSON tools. dumps turns a list/dictionary into text; loads turns JSON text into Python values. JSON uses lowercase false; Python uses False.
blocks.example:
import json
text = json.dumps([{'done': False}])
print(json.loads(text)[0]['done'])  # False
trace: Serialize the Python list into JSON text.
Parse the text back into a list.
The done value returns as a real Python boolean.

blocks.title: Parsing is only the first validation
blocks.idea: Valid JSON can still describe an invalid task. Reuse make_task to validate id,title and minutes. Require actual boolean done, unique ids and exactly the four task fields; reject malformed JSON with ValueError.
trace: Parsing fails before any task is created.
Report ValueError from the import API, then separately validate well-formed data.

steps.title: Next Task Selector
steps.outcome: Learn to search and return early from a list based on conditions.
steps.recap: Keep the earlier functions unchanged. This step adds one new capability to the same planner; the starter contains working earlier functions.

blocks.title: Return the first eligible task
blocks.idea: Scan the list in its existing order. Two conditions must hold: the task is unfinished AND its minutes fit the budget. return immediately stops the function on the first match.
blocks.example:
tasks = [{'minutes': 30, 'done': False}, {'minutes': 20, 'done': False}]
print(tasks[1]['minutes'] <= 25)  # True
trace: The first30-minute task does not fit25.
The planner returns the second task, not the longest task.

blocks.title: Make not-found and invalid-input different
blocks.idea: None means a valid search found no eligible task. ValueError means the budget input is invalid. Budget0 is valid but no positive-duration task fits; negative or non-integer budgets must fail.
blocks.example:
budget = 0
print(budget >= 0)  # True
print(20 <= budget)  # False
trace: Zero is a valid nonnegative budget.
ReturnNone for no fit; reject negative or text budgets.

tracks.title: Study Planner Database and Reports

steps.title: Total Unfinished Planned Minutes
steps.outcome: Aggregate data using GROUP BY and LEFT JOIN to include entities with no associated records.
steps.recap: Combining tables using LEFT JOIN to retain all learners, and SUM to aggregate planned minutes, treating NULL as 0.

blocks.title: Left Join
blocks.idea: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, even if there's no match in the right table.
blocks.example: SELECT l.name, t.title FROM learners l LEFT JOIN tasks t ON l.id = t.learner_id;

blocks.title: Handling NULL with COALESCE
blocks.idea: Use COALESCE to replace NULL with 0 for learners with no tasks.
blocks.example: SELECT COALESCE(SUM(planned_minutes), 0) FROM tasks;

blocks.title: Put the unfinished condition in the join
blocks.idea: Putting t.done=0 in WHERE would remove learners whose joined task is NULL. Put it in ON so every learner remains; then group to add only matching unfinished durations.
blocks.example:
LEFT JOIN tasks t ON l.id=t.learner_id AND t.done=0
-- Meera still appears; her total is0.
trace: An unmatched learner remains and its missing sum becomes0 through COALESCE.

steps.mission: Report all learners.id, learners.name, and the sum of planned_minutes for their unfinished tasks (done = 0) as total_planned. Include learners with no unfinished tasks by returning 0 for them. Order by learners.id.
steps.code:
SELECT l.id, l.name, COALESCE(SUM(t.planned_minutes), 0) AS total_planned
FROM learners l
-- JOIN tasks and group
ORDER BY l.id;
steps.solution: SELECT l.id, l.name, COALESCE(SUM(t.planned_minutes), 0) AS total_planned FROM learners l LEFT JOIN tasks t ON l.id = t.learner_id AND t.done = 0 GROUP BY l.id ORDER BY l.id;

steps.title: Total Studied Minutes
steps.outcome: Pre-aggregate session data to avoid joining complications.
steps.recap: Using Common Table Expressions (CTEs) or Subqueries to aggregate one-to-many relationships before joining to prevent duplication.

blocks.title: Pre-aggregation
blocks.idea: Group child table data before joining to the parent table to avoid multiplying rows.
blocks.example: WITH session_totals AS (SELECT learner_id, SUM(minutes) AS total FROM sessions GROUP BY learner_id) SELECT * FROM session_totals;

blocks.title: Joining Pre-aggregated Data
blocks.idea: Join the summarized data to the main table, handling NULLs for missing data.

steps.mission: Report all learners.id, learners.name, and the sum of their session minutes as total_studied. Use a CTE or subquery to sum sessions per learner first, then LEFT JOIN learners to this result. Ensure those with no sessions return 0. Order by learners.id.
steps.code:
WITH SessionSums AS (
  SELECT learner_id, SUM(minutes) AS total_mins
  FROM sessions
  GROUP BY learner_id
)
SELECT l.id, l.name, COALESCE(s.total_mins, 0) AS total_studied
FROM learners l
-- LEFT JOIN SessionSums
ORDER BY l.id;
steps.solution: WITH SessionSums AS (SELECT learner_id, SUM(minutes) AS total_mins FROM sessions GROUP BY learner_id) SELECT l.id, l.name, COALESCE(s.total_mins, 0) AS total_studied FROM learners l LEFT JOIN SessionSums s ON l.id = s.learner_id ORDER BY l.id;

steps.title: Logging a Session Safely
steps.outcome: Understand transactions, BEGIN/COMMIT, and INSERT statements.
steps.recap: Using transactions to group writes, ensuring database consistency, and verifying changes.

blocks.title: Transactions
blocks.idea: Wrap multiple queries in BEGIN and COMMIT so they succeed or fail together.
blocks.example: BEGIN; INSERT INTO sessions (id, learner_id, day, minutes) VALUES (5, 2, 1, 30); COMMIT;

blocks.title: Rollback deliberately without a foreign-key failure
blocks.idea: In this disposable database, delete only sessions inside the transaction, then ROLLBACK. Deleting learners while child records exist is rejected by foreign keys. A constraint failure does not universally roll back all earlier statements; the caller must handle the transaction.
trace: ROLLBACK undoes the delete; the original count3 remains.

steps.mission: Insert a fictional session (id=4, learner_id=1, day=3, minutes=15) using BEGIN and COMMIT. As your LAST query, SELECT the COUNT(*) as total_sessions and SUM(minutes) as total_minutes from sessions.
steps.solution: BEGIN; INSERT INTO sessions (id, learner_id, day, minutes) VALUES (4, 1, 3, 15); COMMIT; SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_sessions, SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes FROM sessions;

cases.label: Successful transaction
cases.why: The checker reads the actual post-write database: session4 must exist with learner1,day3 and15minutes, and totals must match. Computing adjusted totals without inserting the session will fail.
cases.verifyQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes,(SELECT learner_id FROM sessions WHERE id=4) AS inserted_learner,(SELECT day FROM sessions WHERE id=4) AS inserted_day,(SELECT minutes FROM sessions WHERE id=4) AS inserted_minutes FROM sessions;

steps.title: Study Dashboard
steps.outcome: Combine aggregated CTEs into a unified dashboard.
steps.recap: Using multiple CTEs to independently aggregate distinct child tables, then joining them safely to the parent table.

blocks.title: Multiple CTEs
blocks.idea: Separate CTEs with commas in a single WITH clause.
blocks.example:
WITH task_totals AS (SELECT learner_id,SUM(planned_minutes) AS n FROM tasks WHERE done=0 GROUP BY learner_id),
session_totals AS (SELECT learner_id,SUM(minutes) AS n FROM sessions GROUP BY learner_id)
SELECT * FROM task_totals ORDER BY learner_id;
-- one row per learner with unfinished tasks

blocks.title: Calculating Remaining Time
blocks.idea: This SQLite example uses scalar MAX(x,0) to clamp a negative difference to0. MySQL uses GREATEST(x,0) for this scalar comparison. Planned-minus-studied is a practice reporting rule, not actual completion of a specific task.
blocks.example: SELECT MAX(planned - studied, 0) AS remaining;

steps.mission: Create a coherent dashboard for each learner. Use CTEs to find total_planned (unfinished tasks only) and total_studied (all sessions). Join these to the learners table. Select learners.id, learners.name, total_planned (default 0), total_studied (default 0), and remaining_minutes calculated as MAX(total_planned - total_studied, 0). Order by learners.id.
steps.solution: WITH TaskSums AS (SELECT learner_id, SUM(planned_minutes) AS total_planned FROM tasks WHERE done = 0 GROUP BY learner_id), SessionSums AS (SELECT learner_id, SUM(minutes) AS total_studied FROM sessions GROUP BY learner_id) SELECT l.id, l.name, COALESCE(t.total_planned, 0) AS total_planned, COALESCE(s.total_studied, 0) AS total_studied, MAX(COALESCE(t.total_planned, 0) - COALESCE(s.total_studied, 0), 0) AS remaining_minutes FROM learners l LEFT JOIN TaskSums t ON l.id = t.learner_id LEFT JOIN SessionSums s ON l.id = s.learner_id ORDER BY l.id;
